entries.topic: Cathar origins, beliefs, rites, hierarchy, women, critique of clergy, sacraments, tithes and oaths, surviving texts, historiography

claims.text: Catharism first identifiable c.1143 (Eberwin of Steinfeld report of a group at Cologne); flourished in northern Italy and southern France 12th-14th c.; largely eradicated by c.1350

Bogomil origins: priest Bogomil, 10th-c. Bulgaria, Cosmas's treatise c.970/972; reached the West from Byzantium and the Balkans probably along trade routes; Lambert: substantial transmission of ritual and ideas from Bogomilism to Catharism 'beyond reasonable doubt'

Council of Saint-Félix (1167; charter dated 1167-1172, authenticity debated) attended by Bogomil papa Nicetas; bishopric at Albi c.1165, then Toulouse, Carcassonne, Agen (four by 1200), Razès c.1225; Britannica: 11 bishoprics in France and Italy by 1200
Name 'Cathar' (Greek katharoi, 'pure') coined by Catholic opponents and not used by the accused; they called themselves Good Christians, Good Men, Good Women; also called Albigensians after Albi

Beliefs: good God created spiritual realm; evil principle (Rex Mundi, often Satan, identified with the OT God) created the material world; absolute vs mitigated dualism; souls as fallen angels reincarnated until consolamentum; docetic Christ; cross rejected; OT largely rejected

Gui: they call themselves good Christians who do not swear, lie or kill; call Roman clergy 'Pharisees and false prophets'; deny the host contains Christ's body; call baptismal water material and say churchmen sell it; say confession to Roman priests is useless; refuse to venerate the cross; read Gospels and Epistles in the vernacular

Encyclopedia.com entries: Catharism 'exacted no tithes' and placed no economic restrictions on believers; perfecti rejected violence, jurisdiction and 'the swearing of oaths'; refused obedience to Rome; women perfectae 'performed evangelical, pastoral, and sacramental functions'

Consolamentum: the one sacrament, spiritual baptism by laying on of hands; functioned as baptism, ordination and forgiveness; most believers received it at death; some rites used the Gospel of John or the New Testament; no bread or wine

Lyons Ritual (traditio): elder delivers the Lord's Prayer phrase by phrase; postulant bows (melioramentum), asked 'Do you give yourself to God and the Gospel?', promises 'that you will not lie, that you will not swear, that you will not kill'; never eat or drink without saying the prayer; spiritual baptism by laying on of hands of the Good Men

Credentes made the convenenza, an agreement to receive the consolamentum when dying; perfecti travelled in pairs of the same sex; abstained from meat, eggs, cheese, milk and sex; endura (fast to death after deathbed consolamentum) known in a few late cases, claims of smothering have little evidence

Women could be perfectae and give the consolamentum; lived in communal houses; many widows; late French Cathars taught women must be reborn as men; Esclarmonde of Foix became a Good Woman after raising eight children

Surviving texts: Book of Two Principles (John of Lugio, c.1230/1250), Lyons Ritual (Occitan), Bogomil Interrogatio Iohannis (Secret Supper) brought to Italy c.1190 by Nazarius; most knowledge comes from opponents

Historiography: Moore (War on Heresy) argues Catharism largely contrived from churchmen's imaginations; Pegg calls the crusade genocide, Lerner disputes; Taylor 'post-revisionism'; Rist and Sackville accept an organised heresy existed while Church exaggerated; Sennis ed. Cathars in Question (2016)
Modern: 'Pays cathare' used by the Aude in tourism; Otto Rahn's 1930s Grail theories; Holy Blood and Holy Grail links; Baptist successionism rejected

Audit: the 'exacted no tithes' statement in vt28_ency_cathars is from Beverly Mayne Kienzle's entry 'Cathars' (Encyclopedia of Genocide and Crimes Against Humanity), the only entry on that page to mention tithes; Gui's manual excerpt does not mention tithes. Single secondary source: attribute by name.

Gui (Robinson trans.): they say they are 'good Christians, who do not swear, or lie, or speak evil of others' and 'that they do not kill any man or animal'; accuse churchmen of selling baptismal water 'out of avarice'.

entries.topic: Building the inquisition 1184-1330: Ad abolendam, Vergentis, Lateran IV, Toulouse 1229, Excommunicamus, 1231-33 inquisitors, Ad extirpanda, Gui, Fournier, Bélibaste; the Holy See's later statements

claims.text: Ad abolendam, 4 November 1184, Lucius III at Verona with Frederick I: names Cathars, Humiliati, Poor of Lyon, Arnoldists, Josephines; bishops to visit parishes once or twice a year and put residents on oath; unrepentant/relapsed to lay power for 'animadversio debita'; supporters lose office, trial rights, wills
Vergentis in senium (1199) made heresy lèse-majesté

Council of Toulouse 1229: parish searches, heretics' houses destroyed, laity forbidden to possess OT/NT books except Psalter, Breviary, Hours; 'we most strictly forbid their having any translation of these books'
Excommunicamus (1231): death at the stake for obstinate, prison or canonical penance for repentant, excommunication for helpers; Church handed condemned to secular power

Gregory IX appointed papal inquisitors 1231, mostly Dominicans and Franciscans; 20 April 1233 established inquisition for France, judges initiate proceedings themselves; Madden vs Ullmann views; Talmud confiscation order 1239, mass burning Paris 12 June 1242

Ad extirpanda 15 May 1252, Innocent IV, after murder of Peter of Verona 6 April 1252; authorised torture without loss of life or limb; secular power executes penalties; property in thirds; addressed to Lombardy, Romagna, Treviso march

Bernard Gui (1261-1331), Toulouse: Théry 2010 counts 916 decisions on 636 individuals or communities; c.45 burned (about 6%), mostly relapsed; nearly 30% released; over half prison or penance incl. yellow crosses
Fournier register 1318-1325, bishop of Pamiers, later Benedict XII (1334); Le Roy Ladurie counts 578 interrogations over 370 days; five burned; held in Vatican Library; basis of Montaillou (1975)
Bélibaste betrayed by Arnaud Sicre, burned at Villerouge-Termenès 1321, said to be last Cathar perfect in Languedoc

12 March 2000 Day of Pardon: Ratzinger: 'Even men of the church, in the name of faith and morals, have sometimes used methods not in keeping with the Gospel'; John Paul II 15 June 2004 letter on 1998 symposium volume: repentance for 'intolerance and even the use of violence' in the service of truth; need 'exact knowledge of the facts'

entries.topic: Albigensian Crusade 1208-1229, Béziers, Minerve, Lavaur, Muret, Meaux/Paris 1229, Montségur 1244, death-toll dispute

claims.text: Innocent III (pope 1198) tried preaching missions first, with little success; legate Pierre de Castelnau murdered January 1208 the day after meeting Raymond VI; the pope declared a crusade offering heretics' lands

Béziers 22 July 1209: routiers broke in, people killed in churches; Arnaud Amalric's letter (Aug 1209) says his men put 'almost 20,000' to the sword; Tyerman: true figure 'almost certainly far less'; Marvin: most of the population survived; Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay: 7,000 in the Madeleine church; bishop's list of 222 heretics; Catholics refused to leave
'Caedite eos. Novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius' only in Caesarius of Heisterbach, Dialogue on Miracles, written 1219-1223; doubt whether the abbot said it; Marvin calls the exhortation apocryphal

Carcassonne surrendered 15 August 1209, inhabitants expelled not killed; Simon de Montfort took command; Minerve surrendered 22 July 1210, 140 who refused to recant burned; 1211 Aimery of Montréal's castle (Lavaur) taken, Aimery and knights hanged, several hundred Cathars burned; Muret September 1213 Peter II of Aragon killed; Montfort killed at Toulouse June 1218; Louis VIII 1226; Treaty of Meaux/Paris April 1229 terms

Lateran IV canon 3 (1215): condemned heretics handed to secular rulers; laymen's property confiscated; rulers to swear to exterminate heretics; crusaders against heretics get 'the indulgences and privileges granted to those who go in defense of the Holy Land'
Overall toll: NWE gives one million citing a Time magazine article; no contemporary basis for totals; Pegg calls it genocide, Lerner disputes

Montségur siege May 1243-16 March 1244, Hugues des Arcis vs Pierre-Roger de Mirepoix; surrender terms let all leave who renounced Catharism; two-week truce, some took consolamentum; c.210-215 burned incl. c.190 perfecti, led by bishop Bertrand Marty; 'voluntarily' citation-needed; escape of 3-4 perfecti with treasure 'it has been claimed'
13 May 1239: 183 people burned in Champagne; Peire Autier executed 1310; Bélibaste executed 1321

Castelnau met Raymond VI on 13 January 1208 and was killed the following morning; Carcassonne surrendered 15 August 1209, inhabitants expelled (PVC: naked; Puylaurens: in shifts and breeches); Minerve surrendered 22 July 1210, 140 refusers burned; Muret 12 September 1213, Peter II killed; Montfort killed at Toulouse 25 or 29 June 1218 (sources differ); Louis VIII took the cross January 1226, campaign 1226, died November 1226; Treaty of Paris signed at Meaux 12 April 1229. No overall death toll given.

Siege of Minerve early June to 22 July 1210; 'The 140 people who refused were burned at the stake', footnoted to Peter of les Vaux-de-Cernay (Sibly trans. 1998) p.156; non-perfect Cathars, Catholics and soldiers allowed to leave; few perfect recanted.

Lavaur fell 3 May 1211 after a siege from late March/early April; Montfort ordered Aimery of Montréal and about 80 knights hanged; when the gallows collapsed the rest were put to the sword; Giralda of Laurac thrown into a well and stoned; up to 400 Cathars burned, not offered conversion (Marvin 2008 p.103; Sumption 1999 p.132; Strayer).

Catholic Encyclopedia: Peter of Castelnau assassinated 1208; Béziers and Carcassonne taken 1209; Lavaur fell 1211 'amid dreadful carnage'; Peter of Aragon defeated and killed at Muret 1213; 'Slay all; God will know His own' was 'never pronounced'.

Catholic Encyclopedia: after the conference of Meaux, on 12 April 1229 Raymond VII did public penance in Notre-Dame, Paris, and was absolved; he pledged to demolish the walls of Toulouse and to give his daughter Jeanne in marriage to Alphonse, brother of Louis IX; later accepted the Inquisition at Toulouse.
